facts.claim: Japan attacked the American fleet at Pearl Harbor
facts.context: The attack came on the morning of Sunday 7 December 1941, and Congress declared war the next day.
facts.goDeeper: The whole thing was over in about ninety minutes, and the officer who led the first wave, Mitsuo Fuchida, later became a Christian evangelist and spent years touring the United States.

facts.claim: American bombers flew off an aircraft carrier to strike Tokyo
facts.context: Sixteen B-25s took off from the deck of the Hornet on 18 April 1942 and bombed Tokyo and four other cities.
facts.goDeeper: The bombers were far too big to land back on a carrier, so the crews flew on to China and bailed out or crash-landed in the dark, and most of them got home.

facts.claim: American and Filipino prisoners were marched up the Bataan peninsula
facts.context: After the surrender of Bataan in April 1942, tens of thousands of prisoners were forced to walk north through tropical heat.
facts.goDeeper: The Japanese had planned for perhaps 25,000 prisoners and received roughly three times that number, with nothing ready to feed or move them.

facts.claim: The American fleet broke the Japanese attack at Midway
facts.context: Four Japanese aircraft carriers were lost across a few hours of fighting on 4 June 1942.
facts.goDeeper: American codebreakers had read enough of the Japanese naval code to work out where the blow was coming, and the fleet was waiting.

facts.claim: American fighters ambushed the admiral who had planned Pearl Harbor
facts.context: P-38s flew a long-range intercept over the Solomon Islands on 18 April 1943 and brought Isoroku Yamamoto's aircraft down.
facts.goDeeper: His itinerary had come out of a decoded Japanese signal, and the intercept fell exactly one year to the day after the Doolittle Raid.

facts.claim: MacArthur waded ashore in the Philippines, making good on his promise to return
facts.context: He came ashore at Leyte on 20 October 1944, two and a half years after leaving the islands under orders.
facts.goDeeper: The famous photograph was not staged that first time: the landing craft could not get close enough to the beach, so he had no choice but to wade.

facts.claim: The flag was raised on Mount Suribachi on Iwo Jima
facts.context: Six men put the flag up on the morning of 23 February 1945, four days into the landing.
facts.goDeeper: It was the second flag of that morning; the first was judged too small to be seen from the beaches, so a bigger one was carried up, and that is the one Joe Rosenthal photographed.

source.title: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima

facts.claim: American forces landed on Okinawa
facts.context: The landings began on 1 April 1945 and the fighting ran on for 82 days, the longest battle of the Pacific campaign.
facts.goDeeper: Okinawa was the one Pacific battle fought across an island with a large civilian population living on it, and how it went shaped every argument in Washington about how to end the war.

facts.claim: An atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima
facts.context: A single aircraft dropped the bomb on the morning of 6 August 1945.
facts.goDeeper: The crew had flown from Tinian, some 1,500 miles away, and it was the weather report that morning that settled on Hiroshima rather than another city on the target list.

source.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

facts.claim: Japan signed the surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay
facts.context: The instrument of surrender was signed on the battleship's deck on 2 September 1945.
facts.goDeeper: The ceremony took about twenty-three minutes, and the flag displayed for it had been carried into Tokyo Bay by Commodore Perry's squadron in 1853.

facts.claim: American ships sunk or damaged at Pearl Harbor
facts.context: About 19 ships were sunk or damaged, including all eight battleships that were in the harbour that morning.
facts.goDeeper: All but three of them were raised, repaired and sent back to sea, and several were in Tokyo Bay for the surrender.

facts.claim: Days between the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
facts.context: Hiroshima was bombed on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki three days later, on 9 August.
facts.goDeeper: Nagasaki was not the city chosen when that aircraft took off; cloud over Kokura sent it on to the second name on the list.

source.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

facts.claim: Miles prisoners were marched after the surrender at Bataan
facts.context: The march covered roughly 65 miles up the peninsula, and the men were packed into rail cars for the last stretch.
facts.goDeeper: Filipino villagers along the road threw food to the column knowing they could be punished for it, and a great many did it anyway.

facts.claim: Days the fighting on Iwo Jima lasted
facts.context: The battle ran 36 days, from the landing on 19 February 1945 to the island being declared secure on 26 March.
facts.goDeeper: The photograph everyone knows was taken on the fifth day, with a month of the battle still ahead of the men in it.

facts.claim: Nobody saw the Pearl Harbor attack coming until the first bombs fell
facts.context: A radar station on Oahu picked up the incoming aircraft about an hour ahead and phoned it in; the duty officer took it for a flight of American bombers expected from California.
facts.goDeeper: An American destroyer had already sunk a Japanese midget submarine outside the harbour entrance more than an hour before the first bomb dropped.

facts.claim: The Pacific fleet's aircraft carriers were sunk at Pearl Harbor
facts.context: Not one carrier was there. Two were at sea delivering aircraft to Wake and Midway, and the third was at San Diego.
facts.goDeeper: The Pacific turned out to be a carrier war rather than a battleship war, so the ships that decided it were precisely the ones the attack missed.

facts.claim: Japan's war plan called for an invasion of the American mainland
facts.context: The aim was to take the oil and rubber of Southeast Asia and hold a defensive ring until the United States agreed to terms, not to occupy it.
facts.goDeeper: The mainland was shelled twice by submarines and later reached by paper balloons riding the jet stream, but no landing was ever on the drawing board.

facts.claim: Japanese troops occupied American soil during the war
facts.context: Japan took Attu and Kiska in Alaska's Aleutian Islands in June 1942 and held them for about a year.
facts.goDeeper: When American and Canadian troops finally stormed Kiska in August 1943 the island was empty: the garrison had slipped away by ship under two weeks of fog.

facts.claim: The United States moved people of Japanese descent, most of them citizens, into camps
facts.context: Executive Order 9066, signed in February 1942, led to about 120,000 people being removed from the West Coast; around two-thirds were American citizens.
facts.goDeeper: Congress formally apologised and paid reparations in 1988, more than forty years after the camps closed.

facts.claim: A Japanese soldier was still fighting in the jungle decades after the surrender
facts.context: Hiroo Onoda held out in the Philippines until 1974, when his former commanding officer flew out and formally relieved him of his orders.
facts.goDeeper: He had spent thirty years reading the leaflets announcing the surrender as enemy propaganda, and came home to Japan still in his uniform with his rifle in working order.
